questions.question: _______ means avoiding imports of goods which could be produced in India.
questions.questionHtml: _______ means avoiding imports of goods which could be produced in India.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Self-reliance.

Key Points

  • Self-reliance refers to the ability of a country to produce essential goods and services domestically, minimizing dependency on imports.
  • It aims to strengthen the economic independence of a nation by supporting local industries and reducing the trade deficit.
  • India has emphasized self-reliance through initiatives like "Make in India," which encourages companies to manufacture their products within the country.
  • Self-reliance is also linked to national security, as it ensures that critical supplies are available without dependency on foreign nations.

Additional Information

  • Atmanirbhar Bharat:
    • Launched by the Indian government in 2020, Atmanirbhar Bharat aims to make India a self-reliant nation.
    • The initiative focuses on boosting local manufacturing, promoting local products, and reducing import reliance.
    • It includes measures for various sectors, including agriculture, defense, and MSMEs (Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises).
  • Import Substitution:
    • This economic policy advocates replacing foreign imports with domestic production.
    • It aims to reduce foreign dependency and improve local industry by providing incentives and protections.
  • Economic Growth:
    • Economic growth refers to an increase in the production of goods and services in an economy over a period of time.
    • It is measured by the growth in Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
  • Modernisation:
    • Modernisation involves updating and improving infrastructure, technology, and processes.
    • It aims to enhance efficiency, productivity, and competitiveness in the global market.

questions.solution: Producing finished products from raw materials is the primary activity of the secondary sector. The sector played a significant role in India's industrialization during various Five-Year Plans, focusing on modernization, technology upgrades, and competitiveness in manufacturing.

questions.question: People involved in _________ sector, process the primary materials and convert them into finished goods.

questions.question: Which of the following documents provides a framework, rules and regulations for setting up public and private industries in India?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following documents provides a framework, rules and regulations for setting up public and private industries in India?

options.text: Annual report of the trade union
options.html: Annual report of the trade union

questions.solution:
The correct answer is Industrial policy.

Key Points

  • The Industrial Policy of India provides a framework of rules and regulations for setting up public and private industries.
  • It aims to promote industrial development and economic growth across the country.
  • The policy outlines incentives and support mechanisms for industries to foster entrepreneurship and innovation.
  • It includes measures for liberalization, privatization, and globalization to enhance the competitiveness of Indian industries on a global scale.

Additional Information

  • Industrial Policy
    • The Industrial Policy is formulated by the government to regulate and promote industrial development in the country.
    • It includes guidelines for the establishment and operation of industries, including licensing, foreign investment, and technology transfer.
    • The policy is periodically updated to adapt to changing economic conditions and to address emerging challenges in the industrial sector.
    • Key components of the Industrial Policy include the promotion of small-scale industries, the development of infrastructure, and support for research and development.
  • Union Budget
    • The Union Budget is an annual financial statement presented by the Government of India, detailing its estimated revenue and expenditure for the upcoming fiscal year.
    • It includes proposals for taxation, allocation of funds to various sectors, and measures to promote economic growth and development.
    • The budget is a key policy document that outlines the government's economic priorities and fiscal policies.
  • Company's Financial Statement
    • A company's financial statement is a formal record of its financial activities and performance over a specific period.
    • It includes the balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow statement, providing insights into the company's financial health and profitability.
    • Financial statements are used by stakeholders, including investors, creditors, and regulators, to assess the company's financial position and make informed decisions.
  • Annual Report of the Trade Union
    • The annual report of a trade union provides a summary of its activities, achievements, and financial status for the year.
    • It includes information on membership, collective bargaining agreements, and initiatives undertaken to protect workers' rights and interests.
    • The report serves as a communication tool to keep members informed and engaged with the union's efforts.

questions.question: According to standard census definition, who among the following can be categorised as a main worker in India?

options.text: A person who works for at least 160 days
options.html: A person who works for at least 160 days

options.text: A person who works for at least 183 days
options.html: A person who works for at least 183 days

options.html: A person who works for at least 100 days

Key Points

    • Non-workers.

questions.question: Under the Industrial Policy Resolution 1956, industries in India have been classified into how many categories?
questions.questionHtml: Under the Industrial Policy Resolution 1956, industries in India have been classified into how many categories?
questions.solution: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 classified Indian industries into three categories: Schedule A, reserved exclusively for state control (e.g., defense, railways); Schedule B, allowing both state and private sector participation (e.g., chemicals, fertilizers); and Schedule C, primarily for the private sector with state intervention as needed.

questions.question: Which of the following Acts of 1947 regulates the Indian labour law with regard to trade unions as well as individual workmen?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following Acts of 1947 regulates the Indian labour law with regard to trade unions as well as individual workmen?
questions.solution: The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 regulates labor law in India, covering trade unions and individual workers. It provides compensation for shutdowns, layoffs, or retrenchment, and addresses unfair labor practices. The Indian Councils Act of 1861, Charter Act of 1813, and Rowlatt Act of 1919 also impacted Indian governance.

questions.question: What is the full form of ‘BPO’?
questions.questionHtml: What is the full form of ‘BPO’?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Business Process Outsourcing.

Key Points

  • The full form of BPO is Business Process Outsourcing.
  • BPO involves contracting of specific business tasks, such as customer service or accounting, to a third-party service provider.
  • It allows companies to focus on their core business functions and improve efficiency.
  • BPO services can be categorized into back-office outsourcing, including internal business functions such as human resources or finance, and front-office outsourcing, which includes customer-related services such as contact center services.
  • BPO can help businesses reduce costs, improve service quality, and access global talent.

Additional Information

  • IT Outsourcing
    • Involves subcontracting IT functions to external vendors, including software development, infrastructure management, and technical support.
    • Helps businesses access specialized skills and technologies while reducing costs.
  • Knowledge Process Outsourcing (KPO)
    • Focuses on outsourcing knowledge-intensive tasks such as research, data analysis, and financial consultancy.
    • Requires advanced analytical and technical skills to perform high-level processes.
  • Human Resource Outsourcing (HRO)
    • Involves contracting out human resources functions like recruitment, payroll, and employee training.
    • Allows organizations to streamline their HR processes and focus on strategic HR activities.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT an advantage of privatisation?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following was NOT an advantage of privatisation?

options.text: Additional source of revenue for the government
options.html: Additional source of revenue for the government

questions.solution: Privatisation is the transfer of ownership from the government to the private sector, aimed at improving efficiency and productivity. Key advantages include generating additional revenue for the government, reducing political interference, and enhancing overall performance. It also increases competition by introducing private players into sectors previously dominated by state-run enterprises, leading to better services, more innovation, and greater market efficiency. Reduced competition is not considered an advantage of privatisation. Effective regulation is essential to ensure fair competition and prevent monopolistic practices in privatised sectors.

questions.question: Atal Pension Yojana (APY), a pension scheme for citizens of India, is focused on the _____ sector workers.
questions.questionHtml: Atal Pension Yojana (APY), a pension scheme for citizens of India, is focused on the _____ sector workers.
questions.solution: Atal Pension Yojana (APY), launched in 2015, is a government-guaranteed pension scheme aimed at citizens of India in the unorganized sector. Administered by the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA), it targets individuals aged 18-40 who have a savings bank account. Subscribers receive a minimum guaranteed pension ranging from Rs 1000 to Rs 5000 per month starting at age 60, based on their contributions. In the event of the subscriber's demise, the spouse receives the same pension, and after both pass away, the accumulated pension wealth is returned to the nominee.

questions.question: According to the Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion, which of the following is NOT a core industry?

questions.solution: Core industries are vital for the economy as they provide essential goods and services. The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) in India identifies eight core sectors: cement, coal, crude oil, electricity, fertilizers, natural gas, refinery products, and steel. These sectors constitute 40.27% of the Industrial Production (IIP) weight. questions.question: Which of the following statements about privatisation is FALSE?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following statements about privatisation is FALSE?

options.text: Improved performance is one of the advantages of privatisation.
options.html: Improved performance is one of the advantages of privatisation.

options.text: There is no possibility of exploitation of monopoly power by private companies after privatisation.
options.html: There is no possibility of exploitation of monopoly power by private companies after privatisation.

options.text: There was an increase in the cases of disinvestment after the economic reforms of 1991 as compared to the pre-1991 period.
options.html: There was an increase in the cases of disinvestment after the economic reforms of 1991 as compared to the pre-1991 period.

options.text: Maruti Udyog Limited was a public sector enterprise before the 1991 economic reforms.
options.html: Maruti Udyog Limited was a public sector enterprise before the 1991 economic reforms.

questions.solution: Privatization can result in the exploitation of monopoly power by private companies, particularly in sectors with limited competition, which contradicts the false claim in option 2. Privatization is often linked to improved performance and efficiency of private companies over public sector enterprises. Post-1991 economic reforms in India saw a rise in disinvestment to reduce fiscal burden and enhance public sector efficiency. Maruti Udyog Limited was a public sector entity before these reforms. Privatization aims to improve efficiency, reduce government debt, and boost competitiveness, but it can also lead to job losses, reduced public accountability, and potential exploitation without proper regulations.

questions.question: Licensing policy of the government was primarily aimed to promote _______ .
questions.questionHtml: Licensing policy of the government was primarily aimed to promote _______ .

options.text: development of schools and hospitals in smaller states
options.html: development of schools and hospitals in smaller states

options.text: growth of textiles in southern part of India
options.html: growth of textiles in southern part of India

questions.solution:
The correct answer is regional equality.

Key Points

  • The licensing policy of the government was introduced to regulate the industrial sector and ensure fair competition among businesses. It aimed to control the establishment, expansion, and operation of industries through a licensing system.
  • The primary objective of the licensing policy was to promote regional equality and balanced economic development across different states and regions of the country.
  • It sought to prevent the concentration of industries in a few regions and encourage their dispersal in less-developed areas.
  • Another objective of the licensing policy was to promote import substitution and self-reliance in the economy.
    • It encouraged the production of goods and services within the country and discouraged their importation from abroad.

Additional Information Licensing Policy in India:

  • Industrial licensing in India is a mandatory rule put forth by the government of India for enterprises belonging to certain industries. 
  • The licensing policy was introduced in the Industrial Policy Resolution(IPR) of 1956 to promote regional equality.
  • The rule was passed under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, of 1951, also known as IDR Act.
  • Under this policy, private entrepreneurs were required to obtain a government license before establishing a new industry or expanding an existing one.
  • It also aimed to protect the interests of small-scale industries and prevent the domination of large corporations.
  • It had some drawbacks too as
    • Bureaucratic delays, corruption, and rent-seeking behavior among officials and businessmen were caused by it.
    • It also stifled innovation and efficiency in the industrial sector by creating entry barriers and limiting competition.

questions.question: Small scale industries in 1950 were defined as all those industries in which the maximum investment was ________ lakh rupees.
questions.questionHtml: Small scale industries in 1950 were defined as all those industries in which the maximum investment was ________ lakh rupees.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is five lakh rupees.

Key Points

  • In 1950, small scale industries were defined by the maximum investment limit in plant and machinery.
  • The maximum investment limit for small scale industries was set at five lakh rupees.
  • This definition was intended to encourage the growth and development of small scale industries in India.
  • The investment limit has been revised multiple times over the years to keep up with inflation and economic changes.

Additional Information

  • Small Scale Industries (SSI)
    • Small Scale Industries are industrial undertakings having a fixed investment in plant and machinery, whether held on an ownership basis or by lease or by hire purchase, not exceeding a prescribed limit.
    • SSIs play a crucial role in the economic development of a country due to their contribution to employment, production, and exports.
    • The investment ceiling for SSIs has been revised over the years to reflect changes in economic conditions and industrial growth.
    • In 1950, the investment limit was set at Rs. 5 lakh, but this limit has been raised periodically to accommodate changes in the economy and inflation.
  • Evolution of SSI Definition
    • In 1950: The maximum investment limit was Rs. 5 lakh.
    • In 1966: The investment limit was raised to Rs. 7.5 lakh.
    • In 1985: The investment limit was further raised to Rs. 35 lakh.
    • In 1991: The investment limit was raised to Rs. 60 lakh.
    • In 2006: The Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises Development (MSMED) Act was enacted, which redefined the criteria for categorizing industries.
    • As of now, the MSMED Act of 2006 classifies enterprises based on both investment in plant and machinery/equipment and annual turnover.
  • Importance of SSIs
    • SSIs are vital for economic growth as they provide large-scale employment and contribute significantly to GDP.
    • They help in the utilization of local resources and promote balanced regional development.
    • SSIs contribute to the export earnings of the country and help in the development of entrepreneurial skills among the population.
    • They play a crucial role in the socio-economic development of the country by providing livelihood opportunities.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT the socio-economic objective of Industrial Policy Statement 1980?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following is NOT the socio-economic objective of Industrial Policy Statement 1980?

options.text: Consumer protection against high prices and bad quality
options.html: Consumer protection against high prices and bad quality

options.text: Allowing the maximum foreign direct investment
options.html: Allowing the maximum foreign direct investment

questions.solution:
The correct answer is Allowing the maximum foreign direct investment.

Key Points

  • The Industrial Policy Statement of 1980 emphasized enhancing productivity, employment generation, and the optimum utilization of existing production capacity.
  • It aimed at the promotion of export-oriented industries to improve foreign exchange earnings.
  • The policy also focused on consumer protection against high prices and poor quality of goods.
  • Allowing the maximum foreign direct investment (FDI) was not a primary objective of the Industrial Policy Statement of 1980.

Additional Information

  • Industrial Policy Statement 1980
    • The Industrial Policy Statement of 1980 was introduced to revitalize the Indian economy and make it more competitive.
    • The policy emphasized modernization, technological upgradation, and the development of small and medium enterprises (SMEs).
    • It aimed at achieving higher growth rates and industrial diversification to reduce regional disparities.
    • The policy also sought to improve the efficiency of public sector enterprises and increase their contribution to the economy.
  • Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)
    • FDI involves investment from a foreign entity into the business interests of another country.
    • It is a significant source of non-debt financial resources for the economic development of a country.
    • FDI brings in capital, technology, and expertise, and can lead to job creation and infrastructure development.
    • While FDI is important, it was not the main focus of the Industrial Policy of 1980, which was more oriented towards self-reliance and domestic industrial growth.

questions.question: Which of these is one of the fall out of the industrial licensing system?
questions.questionHtml: Which of these is one of the fall out of the industrial licensing system?

options.text: Large industrial houses availed licenses to prevent competition
options.html: Large industrial houses availed licenses to prevent competition

options.text: Most licenses were used up by backward states
options.html: Most licenses were used up by backward states

options.text: Most licenses were for importing goods
options.html: Most licenses were for importing goods

options.text: Many small private firms appropriated licenses
options.html: Many small private firms appropriated licenses

questions.solution:
The correct answer is Large industrial houses availed licenses to prevent competition.

Key Points

  • The industrial licensing system in India had several fallout, including:
    • Large industrial houses availed licenses to prevent competition: The licensing system was often manipulated by big business houses to prevent new players from entering the market, thereby limiting competition.
    •  Most licenses were used up by backward states: The licensing system favored the established industrial centers, and backward states had a tough time getting licenses.
    • Most licenses were for importing goods: The licensing system was designed to promote domestic manufacturing, and imports were discouraged.
    • Many small private firms appropriated licenses: The licensing system was biased towards large industrial houses, and small private firms had a tough time getting licenses. 

Additional Information

  • Industrial licensing system:
    • The industrial licensing system was introduced in India in 1948 to regulate the growth and development of industries in the country.
    • Under this system, the government issued licenses to companies to set up new industries, expand existing ones, or import technology and machinery.
    • The licensing system was aimed at achieving a balanced regional development of industries, promoting self-sufficiency, and preventing concentration of economic power in a few hands.
    • However, the licensing system was often criticized for being bureaucratic, corrupt, and favoring established players over new entrants.
    • The system was gradually dismantled in the 1990s as part of economic liberalization and reforms.

questions.question: Which of the following led to reservation of industrial activities for private and public sectors for the first time in India?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following led to reservation of industrial activities for private and public sectors for the first time in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956.

Key Points

  • The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 marked a significant step in India's economic planning by reserving certain industries exclusively for the public and private sectors.
  • This policy aimed to accelerate industrialization and create a mixed economy where both public and private sectors would play pivotal roles.
  • Under this resolution, industries were classified into three categories: Schedule A, Schedule B, and Schedule C.
  • Schedule A included industries that would be exclusively owned by the State, Schedule B included industries where the State would play a dominant role, and Schedule C consisted of the remaining industries left to the private sector.
  • The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 laid the foundation for the development of the heavy industries and infrastructure sectors in India.

Additional Information

  • Industrial Policy Resolution, 1948
    • This was the first major industrial policy statement by the Government of India after independence, which aimed to outline the role of the state in industrial development.
    • It categorized industries into four broad areas based on state involvement and control.
  • Industries Development and Regulation Act, 1951
    • This Act provided the framework for the central government to regulate and control the establishment and functioning of industries in India.
    • It aimed to ensure planned and coordinated development of industries across the country.
  • Statement of Industrial Policy, 1945
    • This pre-independence policy aimed to promote industrialization by providing incentives and removing barriers to industrial growth.
    • It focused on reconstruction and development post-World War II.

questions.question: Which of the following industries was NOT in Schedule A of Industrial Policy 1956?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following industries was NOT in Schedule A of Industrial Policy 1956?
questions.solution: Mining of salt was not included in Schedule A of the Industrial Policy 1956, which primarily focused on industries where the state would have exclusive control to ensure their development in a manner that served the national interest. Schedule A listed industries such as air transport, mineral oils, and iron & steel, emphasizing strategic sectors crucial for the country's infrastructure and economic security. The exclusion of salt mining highlights the government's prioritization of industries deemed vital for industrialization and national development during the early years of India's independence.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of a minor industrial region of India?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following is NOT an example of a minor industrial region of India?
questions.solution: Hugli region, is not an example of a minor industrial region in India; instead, it is one of the major industrial regions, known for its jute mills and varied industries around Kolkata. On the other hand, the Durg-Raipur region is noted for its steel plants & cement industry, Ambala-Amritsar for light engineering goods, and the Northern Malabar region for its small-scale industries including coir making & handloom, making them minor industrial areas. These regions highlight India's diverse industrial landscape, ranging from heavy to light and traditional industries.

questions.question: __________ has become the 100 th 'Har Ghar Jal' district in February 2022.
questions.questionHtml: __________ has become the 100<sup>th</sup> 'Har Ghar Jal' district in February 2022.
questions.solution: 'Har Ghar Jal' is a government initiative aimed at providing piped water supply to every household in India by 2024. Chamba, located in Himachal Pradesh, has become the 100th district to achieve the goal of providing piped water supply to every household in February 2022.

questions.question: Hindustan Copper Limited (HCL) was incorporated in the year _________.

questions.solution: Hindustan Copper Limited (HCL) was incorporated on November 9, 1967. questions.solution: SCOMET refers to India's National Export Control List, regulating the export of dual-use items with civilian and military applications. It includes chemicals, organisms, materials, equipment, and technologies. Exporters must obtain a license from DGFT, and exports are either prohibited or authorized under strict conditions.

questions.question: The Industrial Policy Resolution, 1948 mainly categorised the large-scale industries into __________ fragments.
questions.questionHtml: <!-- x-tinymce/html -->The Industrial Policy Resolution, 1948 mainly categorised the large-scale industries into __________ fragments.
questions.solution: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1948 categorized large-scale industries into four main fragments: exclusive state monopoly, basic and strategic industries, industries requiring regulation and control, and other industries. This policy aimed to balance the roles of the public and private sectors in India's industrial development post-independence. It laid the foundation for a mixed economy, promoting both public and private sector collaboration for balanced growth. The resolution emphasized protecting small-scale industries, ensuring fair competition, and shaping India's economic structure. It set the stage for subsequent policies, notably the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956.

questions.question: A small scale industry is defined with reference to the maximum investment allowed on assets which is equal to ________.
questions.questionHtml: A small scale industry is defined with reference to the maximum investment allowed on assets which is equal to ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Rs. 10 crore.

Key Points

  • Small-scale industries:
    • Industries in which manufacturing, production, and servicing of goods are done on a small scale.
    • The total investment of these types of industries does not exceed over 10 crore.
    • Small-scale industries have single ownership.
    • These industries are labor intensive so there is only limited use of technology.
    • These work in local areas and fulfill the demands of locals.

Additional Information

  •  Large-scale industries:
    • ​​have a huge infrastructure, and raw materials and require large numbers of workers.
    • The capital requirement is also large and industries that have fixed assets of more than 10 crores are considered large-scale industries.
    • There are several large-scale industries in India like Iron and steel, automobile, textile, silk industry, etc.
    • These industries use the latest technology and machines.
    • Their contribution to the country's economy is also huge.
    • These require skilled workers that provide employment.

questions.question: With respect to trade and industry, what does 'DPIIT' stand for?
questions.questionHtml: With respect to trade and industry, what does 'DPIIT' stand for?

options.text: Development and Promotion of Industry and International Trade
options.html: Development and Promotion of Industry and International Trade

options.text: Development and Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
options.html: Development and Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade

options.text: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
options.html: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade

options.text: Department for Promotion of Industry and International Trade
options.html: Department for Promotion of Industry and International Trade

questions.solution: DPIIT stands for the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, operating under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government of India. It formulates and implements industrial policies to promote domestic trade and industry. DPIIT monitors the start-up ecosystem and foreign direct investment (FDI) policies. Renamed from the Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion (DIPP) in January 2019, it plays a crucial role in boosting domestic industries and entrepreneurship. The department also manages intellectual property rights (IPR) policies and has introduced initiatives like Make in India, Start-up India, and Ease of Doing Business to facilitate growth.

questions.question: According to a new definition of MSMEs 2020, medium enterprise turnover should NOT exceed how much amount?
questions.questionHtml: According to a new definition of MSMEs 2020, medium enterprise turnover should NOT exceed how much amount?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Rs. 250 crore.

Key Points

  • The new definition of MSMEs was announced in May 2020 by the Government of India.
  • For medium enterprises, the turnover threshold was set at a maximum of Rs. 250 crore.
  • This definition is part of the Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan package to support the economy during the COVID-19 pandemic.
  • The new criteria also include investment limits, with medium enterprises having an investment limit of up to Rs. 50 crore.
  • The revised definition aims to provide a clearer and more inclusive classification for MSMEs, enhancing their growth and development.

Additional Information

  • Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs)
    • MSMEs are categorized based on their investment in plant and machinery or equipment and annual turnover.
    • They play a crucial role in the Indian economy, contributing significantly to employment and GDP.
    • The classification helps in availing benefits such as subsidies, tax exemptions, and easier access to credit.
  • Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan
    • It is a comprehensive economic package aimed at making India self-reliant and resilient.
    • Launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in May 2020, it includes reforms and support for various sectors, including MSMEs.
  • Investment Limits for MSMEs
    • Micro enterprises: Investment up to Rs. 1 crore and turnover up to Rs. 5 crore.
    • Small enterprises: Investment up to Rs. 10 crore and turnover up to Rs. 50 crore.
    • Medium enterprises: Investment up to Rs. 50 crore and turnover up to Rs. 250 crore.
  • Udyam Registration
    • It is an online process for MSMEs to register and obtain a unique identification number.
    • The registration is free of cost and simplifies access to various benefits and schemes.

questions.question: In September 2021,the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) increased the entry age for the National Pension System (NPS) from_______ to ______.
questions.questionHtml: In September 2021,the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) increased the entry age for the National Pension System (NPS) from_______ to ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 65 years; 70 years.Key Points

  • In September 2021, PFRDA increased the entry age for the National Pension System (NPS) from 65 years to 70 years.
  • The maximum age for joining the National Pension Scheme is 70 years.
  • A citizen of India, whether resident or non-resident can join NPS (National Pension Scheme).

Additional Information

  • Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority:
    • It is the statutory authority established by an enactment of the Parliament, to regulate, promote and ensure orderly growth of the National Pension System (NPS).
    • It works under the Department of Financial Services under the Ministry of Finance.
    • Functions:
    • It performs the function of appointing various intermediate agencies like Pension Fund Managers, Central Record Keeping Agency (CRA), etc.
    • It develops, promotes, and regulates the pension industry under the NPS and also administers the APY.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a joint sector industry?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following is an example of a joint sector industry?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Oil India Limited.

Key Points

  • Oil India Limited (OIL) is a joint sector company where the government collaborates with private entities to run the business.
  • The company was established in 1959 and is a key player in the oil and gas sector in India.
  • OIL is involved in the exploration, development, and production of crude oil and natural gas, transportation of crude oil, and production of LPG.
  • The Government of India holds a significant share in the company, making it a joint sector enterprise.

Additional Information

  • Joint Sector Enterprises
    • These are businesses where the government collaborates with private firms to undertake the establishment and operations of industries.
    • The primary objective is to combine the resources and expertise of both sectors for effective and efficient management.
    • Such collaborations often aim at reducing the risk involved and increasing the capital investment for large-scale projects.
    • Examples include Oil India Limited and Maruti Udyog Limited.
  • Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL)
    • It is a state-owned aerospace and defense company based in India.
    • HAL is primarily involved in the design, fabrication, and assembly of aircraft, jet engines, helicopters, and their spare parts.
    • It operates under the administrative control of the Ministry of Defence.
  • National Highway Authority of India (NHAI)
    • NHAI is an autonomous agency of the Government of India, responsible for the management of a network of over 50,000 km of National Highways.
    • It operates under the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways.
    • NHAI is involved in the construction, management, and maintenance of highways.
  • Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL)
    • SAIL is one of the largest state-owned steel-making companies in India and one of the top steel makers in the world.
    • It operates under the Ministry of Steel, Government of India.
    • SAIL produces iron and steel at five integrated plants and three special steel plants, located principally in the eastern and central regions of India.
